title: Physical and chemical changes
status: draft: written 18 Nov 2026 offline for Grade 8 Integrated Science; not yet checked by a CBC Integrated Science teacher; not loaded by the live tutor
notes: Learners act out the particles: standing close and shaking (solid), close and sliding past (liquid), spread out and moving fast (gas). The teacher boils pure and salty water with a thermometer. Physical and chemical changes are sorted from real examples: melting wax, dissolving sugar, burning paper, rusting nails, cooking an egg.

skills.key_step: The child describes the particles in each state: solid (close, in fixed places, vibrate), liquid (close, slide past one another), gas (far apart, move fast in all directions), and explains shape and flow from this.

floor.prerequisite: Knows the names of the changes of state.
floor.question: What is the change from liquid to gas called?

representations: three boxes of dots: packed, close and jumbled, far apart
a syringe of air squeezed and a syringe of water
steps: Solid: packed in rows, vibrating in place.
Liquid: close, sliding past each other.
Use the picture to explain: gases can be squeezed, liquids flow.

board.do: Draw three boxes: packed dots, close jumbled dots, few scattered dots.
Wait for "the particles are far apart".

misconceptions.ask: Do the particles in our acted solid shake?
misconceptions.repair: Solid particles vibrate in fixed places.

misconceptions.ask: Why can a syringe of air be pushed in?
Why does water take the shape of the jug?
misconceptions.repair: Liquid particles slide past each other.

misconceptions.ask: In the acting, did anyone grow?
misconceptions.repair: Particles move more and spread out; they do not grow.

checks.question: Why can a gas be squeezed but a solid cannot?
checks.answer: gas particles are far apart; solid particles are packed close

checks.question: How do the particles in a liquid move?
checks.answer: they are close and slide past one another

skills.key_step: The child says impurities raise the boiling point and lower the melting point, and uses a fixed boiling or melting point to test purity.

floor.prerequisite: Knows the particle picture of the states.
floor.question: How do the particles in a solid move?

representations: pure and salty water boiled with a thermometer (teacher)
salt on ice in a cup
a chart: pure, impure, boiling and melting
steps: Pure water boils at 100 degrees (at sea level) and melts at 0.
Salt on ice: it melts below 0.
A different fixed point shows an impurity.
contexts: checking water purity in a laboratory

board.do: Draw two thermometers: pure water and salty water, both boiling.
Ask which shows the higher reading.

misconceptions.ask: What did the thermometer show for the salty water?
Why does salt melt ice on roads?

misconceptions.repair: Impurities change boiling and melting points.
The fixed point shows purity, not the look.

checks.question: What does an impurity do to the boiling point of water?
How can you test whether a sample of water is pure?
checks.answer: check that it boils at 100 degrees (at sea level) or freezes at 0

skills.key_step: The child tells a physical change (no new substance, often reversible: melting, dissolving, freezing) from a chemical change (new substance, hard to reverse: burning, rusting, cooking), and gives applications of changes of state.

floor.prerequisite: Knows the names of the changes of state.
floor.question: What is the change from solid to liquid called?

representations: real examples on a tray: wax, sugar, paper, an old nail, an egg
the questions "New substance? Can it go back?"
steps: Ask: is a new substance made?
Ask: can it easily go back?
No and yes: physical. Yes and no: chemical.
Signs of chemical change: gas, colour change, heat or light given out.

board.do: Write melting wax, burning paper, dissolving sugar, rusting nail.

board.say: Can the ash become paper again?

board.do: Ask the child to sort the four.

misconceptions.ask: Is the melted wax still wax?
Can the ash turn back into wood?

listen_for: a physical change makes something new
misconceptions.ask: Is sugar water still sugar and water?
misconceptions.repair: Only a chemical change makes a new substance.

listen_for: the sugar is gone, so it is chemical
misconceptions.ask: What was left on the dried saucer?

checks.question: Is rusting a physical or a chemical change?
Give one sign that a chemical change has happened.
checks.answer: a new substance, a gas given off, a colour change, heat or light given out
